629516ed21.q: What is prostate cancer and how does the prostate gland function in the male body?
629516ed21.a: The prostate gland is a gland that only men have, located between the bladder and the top of the penis, which produces, stores and secretes semen. Prostate cancer occurs when cells within that organ lose their control mechanisms and keep growing without any stop sign, resulting in an overgrowth of the prostate gland.

68ced60f7e.q: At what age should men without family history begin PSA screening for prostate cancer?
68ced60f7e.a: If you have a family history, men should start PSA screening at over 40 years old. If you don't have a family history, the general recommendation is probably over 50 years old. The average age of men that get prostate cancer is actually in their 70s.

7fcb11c617.q: What is the diagnostic process after an elevated PSA blood test result for prostate cancer?
7fcb11c617.a: After an elevated PSA is confirmed, a GP typically refers the patient to a urologist who takes history and performs a digital rectal exam. If abnormal, an MRI scan follows to check for enlarged prostate or suspicious lesions. If abnormal areas are found on MRI, the next step is usually a biopsy—a day case surgery where multiple tissue cores are taken from throughout the prostate gland and sent to the lab.

295955d9b3.q: What is a PSMA PET scan and how does it differ from an MRI scan in prostate cancer detection?
295955d9b3.a: A PSMA PET scan is a specific prostate cancer PET scan that looks at the whole body from top to toe, whereas the MRI really is just focusing on the prostate and the pelvic area. The PET scan gives a much more sensitive pickup rate of any prostate cancer that could be anywhere in the body and can pick up abnormal lymph glands even if they look normal on an MRI scan.

f: A PSMA PET scan is a specific prostate cancer PET scan that examines the whole body from top to toe, whereas an MRI scan focuses only on the prostate and pelvic area. The PSMA PET scan provides a much more sensitive detection rate for prostate cancer that could be located anywhere in the body and can identify abnormal lymph glands even when they appear normal on an MRI scan. This comprehensive imaging capability makes the PSMA PET scan particularly valuable for assessing the extent of disease spread.

The two scans serve different purposes in prostate cancer diagnosis and staging. After a biopsy confirms prostate cancer, doctors typically order a PSMA PET scan to help determine the cancer's risk level and whether it has spread beyond the prostate gland. The MRI's focused view on the prostate gland itself helps identify abnormal lesions within the organ, while the PET scan's whole-body assessment reveals whether cancer has metastasized to lymph nodes or other distant sites, enabling doctors to decide between active surveillance, surgery, or radiation treatment.

c4a6b9b703.q: What is the recurrence rate for prostate cancer after surgical removal with clear margins?
c4a6b9b703.a: It's definitely not common—about one in three patients actually require further treatment after surgery. Even in situations where people have positive surgical margins, only one in three of those people reach a point where they need radiation treatment. So there's a very good chance that with surgery people can be completely cured.

d8b8e791d0.q: What are the three main types of skin cancer in Queensland?
d8b8e791d0.a: Queensland has the highest rate of skin cancers in the world. The most common type is basal cell carcinoma, typically appearing as a shiny nodule on the head and neck area. The second most common is squamous cell cancer, which presents as crusty raised plaques in sun-exposed areas. Melanoma is less common but more serious and aggressive, behaving very differently from the other two types.

67481f85a3.q: What sun protection methods does Icon Cancer Centre Toowoomba recommend for skin cancer prevention?
67481f85a3.a: Dr. Kumar recommends the slip, slop, slap approach: slip into lightweight, fully clothed shirts and long pants when outdoors; slop on sunscreen of SPF 50 and above, paying special attention to forgotten areas like behind the ears, feet, and neck; and slap on a wide brim hat for more coverage than a cap. Additionally, seek shade between 10am and 3pm when UV index is highest, avoid reflective surfaces like sand or concrete, and wear UV-rated sunglasses.

62f54cac25.q: What are the main risk factors for developing head and neck cancer?
62f54cac25.a: The primary risk factors include heavy smoking history with cannabis or tobacco, heavy alcohol use beyond recommended levels, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, poor dental hygiene and neglected oral ulcers. HPV is increasingly seen in younger patients who are not heavy smokers or drinkers but have contracted the virus, which can present as head and neck cancer.

a05a973457.q: What radiation therapy techniques does Icon Cancer Centre Toowoomba use for head and neck cancer?
a05a973457.a: Icon Cancer Centre Toowoomba primarily uses volumetric arc therapy (VMAT), a highly specialized radiation technique designed to target tumor sites while sparing organs at risk and important structures in the head and neck to limit short and long-term side effects. They also offer intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) less frequently, and stereotactic guided radiation therapy, though evidence for the latter in head and neck cancer is limited.

0784abdf2a.q: What is radiotherapy and how is it used to treat breast cancer?
0784abdf2a.a: Radiotherapy uses high energy X-rays to destroy microscopic cancer cells by damaging their DNA so they cannot grow or multiply. For breast cancer, it is delivered after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk, sometimes after mastectomy, and in metastatic disease to shrink tumors and relieve pain. It is part of a multidisciplinary treatment approach.

6bf946a88a.q: What is the typical sequencing and timing of breast cancer treatment combining surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy?
6bf946a88a.a: Historically surgery came first, followed by chemotherapy or radiotherapy based on pathology. Nowadays, certain breast cancers benefit from chemotherapy first, then surgery, then radiation. The timing to start radiation after surgery is generally six to eight weeks, and post-chemotherapy is about three to four weeks.

05a4a0cd79.q: What are the common side effects of breast radiotherapy and how do they vary by skin type?
05a4a0cd79.a: Common side effects include skin irritation, itching, mild pain, and tiredness during the treatment period. Patients with fairer complexions experience more obvious reactions like redness, peeling and dryness, while patients with darker skin tones may show more skin darkening. However, skin color alone does not determine sensitivity; genetics, dose per fraction, body mass index, and smoking are key factors.

d4f15507d4.q: How long does a typical radiation treatment schedule last and how many sessions do breast cancer patients receive?
d4f15507d4.a: Modern treatment trends favor shorter regimens. Treatment is generally given over three weeks on weekdays only, and in some cases can be as short as five days, with no compromise to treatment outcomes. This differs from ten to fifteen years ago when patients received treatment over five to six weeks. Trials in the UK, Canada, America and Australia support these shorter courses.

a8f4adec7e.q: What are the late side effects of breast radiotherapy and what is the risk of secondary cancer development?
a8f4adec7e.a: Late side effects include skin fibrosis and impact on underlying organs like the heart and lung. There is a rare but serious risk of radiation-induced second cancer in the treatment area, generally occurring 10 to 15 years after treatment, such as sarcomas. However, with modern techniques used in Toowoomba, the cardiovascular disease risk is very small, and the benefits of radiation treatment far outweigh the risks.
